messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette is missing some reported symptoms or demographic details. Rewrite it to include everything.

Previous vignette:
# Marcus

Marcus was forty-one when he walked into the clinic, though the way he carried himself—shoulders rounded, eyes that seemed to look past rather than at you—made him appear older. He had come because his ex-wife had finally stopped answering his calls, and his supervisor had given him a written warning about missing work. Both developments felt inevitable to Marcus, like dominoes he had watched falling but could not catch. What he wanted to understand, though he couldn't quite articulate it, was why the ground beneath his life had become so unstable.

Seven years earlier, Marcus had been working on a residential renovation crew in Trenton when the accident happened. It was a Tuesday in late September, the kind of clear morning that felt like nothing bad could occur. He and three other men were framing out the second floor of a colonial-style home. Marcus was on the ground, cutting lumber, when he heard the shout—a sound of surprise rather than pain at first. He looked up to see his friend and crew chief, David, falling backward off the scaffolding. The image burned itself into Marcus's mind in fragments: David's arms windmilling, the terrible geometry of his body striking the concrete foundation, the specific smell of dust and blood and something else Marcus couldn't name but could taste on his tongue—copper mixed with something acidic, something he later realized was his own fear. The sound David made when he landed was not a scream but a wet, final silence. Marcus had stood there, hands still gripping the saw, unable to move, unable to stop what had already stopped.

David died three days later in the hospital. The investigation found that someone had failed to secure the scaffolding properly. Marcus had checked it that morning—he was always careful—but not thoroughly enough. That was the thought that had lived in his chest ever since: he could have caught it. He could have stopped it. But he hadn't, because he was not the kind of person who stopped bad things. The world, he had come to understand, was not a place where competence or vigilance mattered. Bad things happened, and you stood there helpless, and then you lived with it.

For the first two years after David's death, Marcus had drunk heavily. When the drinking stopped working—when it no longer dulled the sensory flashes that arrived without warning—he had found other ways to absent himself. He began gambling, first online, then at the casino in Atlantic City. The rush of placing a bet, the possibility of a win, the total absorption of his attention—these things worked better than alcohol. They gave him permission to not be present in his body, to not feel the weight of his own inadequacy. He would drive to Atlantic City on his days off and lose money he didn't have, and in those hours at the table, he was not the man who had failed to save his friend.

At work, Marcus had become someone his crew barely recognized. He had always been steady, patient with younger workers, someone who could defuse tension with a joke. Now he moved through job sites in a kind of controlled fury that he never allowed himself to express. When a subcontractor made a mistake, or when someone on his crew cut a corner, Marcus would feel the rage rise in his throat like bile, and he would swallow it down. He would excuse himself, walk to his truck, sit in the cab with his hands gripping the steering wheel until his knuckles went white. To let that anger out felt dangerous to him—if he started, he believed, he would not be able to stop. And if he lost control, he might hurt someone, and then he would be the kind of man who broke things, the kind of man who made things worse. So he kept it sealed inside, a pressure that never released.

The memory of David's fall came without warning and with complete sensory vividness. A smell—dust after rain, or sometimes the particular copper-iron scent of raw meat at a grocery store—would transport Marcus instantly back to that moment. He could taste it again, that acidic-metallic compound that coated his mouth. He would see the image: David's body, the angle of his fall, the terrible stillness. These were not thoughts that Marcus could reason with or dismiss. They were pictures that played without his permission, and they came with a certainty that he was powerless to prevent the next catastrophe, that he was fundamentally inadequate to the task of keeping people safe.

When these memories arrived, Marcus would sometimes deliberately try to leave his body, to dissociate, to create distance between himself and the sensation. He had learned to do this—to mentally step outside himself, to watch himself from a remove, to blank out the sensory details. It worked sometimes. Other times, he would end up at the casino instead, or sitting in his truck for hours, unable to account for the time.

His ex-wife, Jennifer, had tried for three years to reach him. She had suggested therapy, medication, anything. But Marcus had come to believe that there was nothing to fix, nothing to understand—only a truth he had learned: that the world was fundamentally unsafe, that he was inadequate to protect anything or anyone, and that the best he could do was try not to hurt anyone else while he waited for the next inevitable disaster. When Jennifer finally left, it had felt like confirmation rather than surprise.

Now, sitting in the clinic, Marcus was not sure what he wanted. He was certain that talking about what happened would not change the fact of it. He was certain that he could not stop bad things from happening. But something had shifted. His supervisor's warning had been the final weight on a scale that had been tipping for years. He had come because he had nowhere else to go, and because somewhere beneath the conviction of his own helplessness, there was a small, terrified part of him that wondered if he was wrong.

Missing items that MUST appear in the rewrite:
MISSING FROM VIGNETTE:
- Age discrepancy: Patient is 39, vignette states Marcus is 41: The vignette opens with 'Marcus was forty-one when he walked into the clinic,' but the patient's reported age is 39. This is a material demographic inconsistency that violates the accuracy requirement for the vignette.

Rewrite the full vignette (4–5 paragraphs, third person) incorporating all missing items as lived clinical experience.
Preserve all content from the previous vignette that was already correct — only add what is missing.
